newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Healthcare UK voters' big worry - Reuters/NOP.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Healthcare UK voters' big worry - Reuters/NOP.

text.p: A gnawing anxiety over the state of the health service will be the crucial issue weighing on voters' minds as they enter Britain's polling booths on Thursday, an eve-of-election opinion poll for Reuters showed on Wednesday.

The polling organisation NOP asked 1,093 people in 52 constituencies across Britain on Tuesday what they saw as the most important factors influencing their vote this election. The National Health Service (NHS) came top of the list, mentioned by 47 percent of those surveyed.

"There is a very considerable concern amongst people about whether they can rely on the health service to give them the appropriate treatment at the appropriate time," said Eric Shaw, senior lecturer in politics at the University of Stirling. "People are prepared to pay more in taxes to improve the service," he added.

The health service is seen as one of Labour's trump cards. Labour, which enjoyed a 22-point lead over the Conservatives in the poll, has promised to cut the money spent on administration, channelling it instead to patient care.

John Major's Conservatives have said they will increase the real resources given to the NHS and bring in private-sector investment, while the Liberals plan free eye and dental checks and more NHS staff, paid for partly by more tax on cigarettes.
Some 33 percent of respondents said the parties' education policies would influence the way they intended to vote on Thursday.

Labour leader Tony Blair has called education his "number one priority". But only Paddy Ashdown's Liberal Democrats have set out clear spending plans, promising to pour an extra two billion pounds ($3.3 billion) a year into education by upping the basic rate of income tax by a penny.

"People feel that there are serious problems in the British education system. Our international performance is not good. Education is not working as well as it should," said David Denver, lecturer in politics at the University of Lancaster. "The issue is more likely to benefit Labour and the Lib Dems. People like the idea of the government spending more money."

Unemployment was another voter concern with 26 percent of respondents worried about job security. The increase in short-term, part-time and contract work and a reduction of the number claiming unemployment benefit, has led to many people feeling unsafe in their jobs, political experts said.
The economy was also seen as an important factor by 23 percent of those surveyed, closely followed by the feeling that "It's time for a change."
"People are just thoroughly fed up with the government, its general approach and the personalities involved," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester.
Denver said: "'Time for a change' is a diffuse issue, a vague feeling which is still there, but people are concentrating more on the issues."

Perhaps surprisingly, the recent furore over Britain's relations with Europe, an argument that has fragmented the Conservative Party, played a minor role, with just 19 percent of respondents saying it would influence their vote.
